title: Big Tech lines up in support of open-weight AI - Axios
description:
Throughout the weekend, more companies joined, including Google and OpenAI, despite both companies offering mostly closed models.
Zoom in: Nvidia doubled down Monday by launching the Open Secure AI Alliance, which calls for open research and regulatory support for open models as "defensive assets, not liabilities."
"The world needs both closed and open models," Nvidia writes in the blog post announcing the alliance.
Frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI generate revenue by selling access to proprietary models that only they have the keys to.
Case in point: Anthropic has emerged as the industry's clearest public skeptic of frontier open-weight AI.
text:
The big picture: The renewed debate over open source is the latest Silicon Valley division in the AI race.

Catch up quick: Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, Palantir and dozens of other companies signed an industry letter Friday backing the open-weight AI ecosystem.

Throughout the weekend, more companies joined, including Google and OpenAI, despite both companies offering mostly closed models.

Anthropic — which also sells closed models — has not signed the agreement.

Zoom in: Nvidia doubled down Monday by launching the Open Secure AI Alliance, which calls for open research and regulatory support for open models as "defensive assets, not liabilities." Founding members include SpaceXAI, Thinking Machines and over 25 other companies.

Open development "produces stronger defense," Nvidia's VP of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano told Axios.

Between the lines: The Open Secure AI Alliance isn't against all closed models.

"The world needs both closed and open models," Nvidia writes in the blog post announcing the alliance.

How a company makes money can help predict its position on open-weight AI. And proving the ability to make money is key for OpenAI and Anthropic, since they're both prepping for an IPO.

Frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI generate revenue by selling access to proprietary models that only they have the keys to.

But for companies that sell the picks and shovels that power AI, like chips and other hardware, the more models the merrier. Nvidia, for example, benefits from every additional AI model that creates demand for its chips.

State of play: The industry push comes as the Trump administration debates how to respond to rapidly improving Chinese open-weight AI models which have surged in popularity.

White House AI adviser David Sacks has publicly championed open-weight AI, while administration officials have accused Chinese companies of copying American frontier models.

Case in point: Anthropic has emerged as the industry's clearest public skeptic of frontier open-weight AI.

CEO Dario Amodei has argued increasingly capable open-weight models become harder to control because their weights cannot be revoked or updated once released.

The argument got a live test this month when OpenAI models broke out of a testing sandbox, exploited a zero-day and breached Hugging Face's production systems while trying to cheat a benchmark.

Reality check: "Open models, like any powerful technology, can be misused — including attempts to weaken safeguards or repurpose capabilities for cyber attacks — but those risks are not unique to open systems, and they must be managed wherever advanced AI is deployed," Nvidia says in the blog.

"When defenders cannot inspect, adapt and run advanced AI on their own infrastructure, their ability to respond is constrained at exactly the moment speed matters most," the blog says.

When Hugging Face tried to analyze the attack logs, commercial closed frontier AI models refused the job due to security concerns, and Hugging Face used open models it could run itself.

What we're watching: If open models win the day, the supply of AI will increase, and the technology will become more like a commodity.

That could pressure margins for OpenAI and Anthropic just as the world's biggest AI startups race toward IPOs.

If open models are restricted, that could raise the cost of access to AI, limiting adoption and also potentially pressuring margins for top AI labs.

name: Agilent
title: Once Blocked by Trump on Qualcomm, Broadcom Rises as Key Anti-Nvidia Force
description:
According to companiesmarketcap.com, a website that tracks U.S. market capitalizations, Broadcom's market cap stood at $1.82 trillion (about 2,669.03 trillion won) as of the 26th (local time).
Excluding TSMC, a Taiwanese company, Broadcom ranks as the second-largest U.S. semiconductor company after Nvidia ($5 trillion).
Avago acquired Broadcom for $37 billion in 2015 and changed its name to that of the acquired company, Broadcom.
However, President Trump rejected the deal on national security grounds, calling Broadcom a Singaporean company close to China.
As Broadcom leads the custom semiconductor market, it is putting Nvidia on edge.
text:
Broadcom is once again drawing attention following an artificial intelligence (AI) summit held over the past weekend in San Francisco. Hock Tan, Broadcom's chief executive officer (CEO) and an immigrant from Malaysia, has grown the company through aggressive mergers and acquisitions (M&A) into the largest force leading the anti-Nvidia front.

According to companiesmarketcap.com, a website that tracks U.S. market capitalizations, Broadcom's market cap stood at $1.82 trillion (about 2,669.03 trillion won) as of the 26th (local time). That ranks seventh, following Nvidia, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Amazon and TSMC. Excluding TSMC, a Taiwanese company, Broadcom ranks as the second-largest U.S. semiconductor company after Nvidia ($5 trillion).

Broadcom traces its roots to the semiconductor products division that Hewlett-Packard (HP) operated starting in 1961. This organization continued for nearly 40 years before being absorbed into Agilent, which was spun off from HP's semiconductor business in 1999. Kohlberg Kravis Roberts (KKR), the world's largest private equity fund (PEF), and Silver Lake Partners acquired Agilent for $2.66 billion at the end of 2005 and launched it as Avago Technologies, headquartered in Singapore. Avago acquired Broadcom for $37 billion in 2015 and changed its name to that of the acquired company, Broadcom. The CEO of Avago at the time was Hock Tan, who has been in charge of management for 20 years, first at Avago from 2006 and then at Broadcom.

Tan was born in Penang, Malaysia, in 1953 and moved to the United States in 1971 at the age of 18 as a first-generation immigrant. He graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Harvard Business School.

Like a private equity fund, he grew Broadcom by attaching companies from the same industry. He acquired LSI, a system semiconductor specialist, for $6.6 billion in 2014; Brocade, a maker of network equipment such as routers and switches, for $5.9 billion in 2017; and VMware, a virtualization platform company, for $69 billion in 2023. Broadcom's market cap, which stood at around $2.7 billion in the Avago era, surpassed $1 trillion in 2024.

Tan also flexibly resolved conflict with the Donald Trump administration. In 2017, early in Trump's first term, Broadcom attempted to swallow Qualcomm for $117 billion. The aim was to acquire Qualcomm, which was competing with China's Huawei in the fifth-generation (5G) mobile communications infrastructure market, and expand its business into mobile chips. However, President Trump rejected the deal on national security grounds, calling Broadcom a Singaporean company close to China. A few months later, in November 2017, Tan appeared alongside President Trump at the White House and announced that Broadcom would relocate its headquarters to Silicon Valley in the United States.

At the time of the announcement, Tan said, "My mom would never have imagined that I would stand next to the U.S. president at the White House," drawing a smile from President Trump. The scene in which President Trump, watching the announcement from behind, replied, "My mom too (would never have known I would become president and enter the White House)," became a major talking point.

Though it lost Qualcomm, the AI boom was an enormous opportunity for Broadcom. Broadcom's core business had long been networking, but as demand for application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) optimized for inference surged from last year, the chip capabilities Broadcom had built over 60 years began to shine. To counter Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs), big tech companies lined up to commission Broadcom to design their own chips. Broadcom oversees silicon manufacturing, power and thermal management, and memory integration, as well as final foundry (contract semiconductor manufacturing) preparation.

Google, the leader in this field, also chose Broadcom. Broadcom is participating in the development of Google's ASIC, the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). OpenAI also announced in October last year that it would cooperate with Broadcom to develop custom chips, and in June this year, OpenAI's first proprietary inference-only chip, "Jalapeno," was unveiled. Anthropic, OpenAI's rival, signed a contract with Google and Broadcom in April this year to secure gigawatt-scale TPU capacity. Meta also entrusted the design to Broadcom in March this year when it unveiled four products in its Meta Training and Inference Accelerator (MTIA) lineup, including the MTIA 300, 400, 450 and 500.

As Broadcom leads the custom semiconductor market, it is putting Nvidia on edge. According to Forbes, Nvidia's top-spec GPUs are priced at $30,000 to $40,000 each, while custom TPUs in which Broadcom is involved can be purchased for $12,000, and the energy efficiency of TPUs in inference tasks is 67% higher than comparable GPUs. At the unveiling of Jalapeno last month, Tan boasted of the company's technology, saying it "has performance on par with Nvidia's Blackwell chips or Google's TPUs."

name: Adobe
title: Adobe Kept Hearing the Same Complaint From Creators. It Changed Its Strategy Because of It
description:
Creator as founder, not creator as talent This is what Adobe kept hearing.
Once a company hears its audience that way, the product problem changes.
Adobe’s latest Creators’ Toolkit Report surveyed more than 16,000 creators, and 87 percent of those using creative AI said it had accelerated their business or audience growth.
A company that hears “creator” as one persona builds for a person who doesn’t exist.
A company that hears how wide the category has grown builds for the spread, and reaches more people because of it.
text:
Creator as founder, not creator as talent

This is what Adobe kept hearing. “When we talk to them, we consistently hear that they want to spend less time on day-to-day tasks that come with running a business,” says Mike Polner, vice president of product marketing for creators at Adobe. His read on who these people actually are matters, because it shapes what a company decides to build. “Creators of today are entrepreneurs and small business owners, often wearing multiple hats and managing every part of their business.”

That framing means switching from the creator as talent to the creator as a founder. Once a company hears its audience that way, the product problem changes. The job stops being “help people make prettier things” and becomes “give people their time back so they can run the business only they can run.”

The numbers say the shift is real and widely felt. Adobe’s latest Creators’ Toolkit Report surveyed more than 16,000 creators, and 87 percent of those using creative AI said it had accelerated their business or audience growth. The point worth sitting with is tied to business growth. These are people measuring a tool by what it did for their company, not their content.

The range is the point

Gigi Robinson is a useful person to listen to here, because her history with the tools is long enough to see the change clearly. She has used Adobe products since she was ten or eleven, through high school at LaGuardia and a BFA and master’s at USC, into her current work as founder of Hosts of Influence. What’s different now isn’t the software she opens. It’s how much of her business the same suite touches. In the past year, her work with Adobe has run through speaking, hosted events, a newsletter, a podcast, and social content, which is to say the actual sprawl of a creator’s operation rather than a single lane.

“It has empowered me to be a better speaker, use the products to promote creative development, and ultimately become a better entrepreneur while inspiring others to do the same,” Robinson says. Entrepreneur is the word doing the work.

She noticed something at Cannes that gets at why listening to this audience is harder than it sounds. The people in the room labeled “creator” had—on paper—almost nothing in common with each other. Some made mobile-only content. Others ran full film and video crews. Lifestyle and travel creators sat beside deeply technical ones, all using the same underlying tools to make completely different work. Her conclusion was that the range is the point. A company that hears “creator” as one persona builds for a person who doesn’t exist. A company that hears how wide the category has grown builds for the spread, and reaches more people because of it.

title: Amazon and Microsoft are spending $400 billion on AI—and investors are low on patience
description:
While Amazon and Microsoft have been locked in the cloud battle for years, the pressure has never been higher and investor patience has never been more unpredictable.
Revenue growth, profit margins, and customer backlogs at Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure will be closely scrutinized.
Between them, Microsoft and Amazon own half the cloud market, with Amazon’s 28% market share topping Microsoft’s 21%, according to Synergy data.
Microsoft isn’t issuing new bonds and is instead funding a buildout of roughly $35 billion per quarter from its operating cash flow.
With both Microsoft and Amazon neck-and-neck, the two cloud businesses are are selling out of everything they can build.
text:
Each company is set to spend roughly $200 billion this year building out its data centers—an unprecedented level of investment—in a frenzied bid to keep up with demand for AI services and to avoid getting overtaken by other cloud rivals like Google. The cloud titans have also forged partnerships and deals with the big AI model makers, creating a web of shifting alliances that each hopes could reshape the competitive landscape.

This week, investors will get an important update on the state of this epic cloud rivalry, when Microsoft reports its quarterly earnings on Wednesday and Amazon follows suit on Thursday. While Amazon and Microsoft have been locked in the cloud battle for years, the pressure has never been higher and investor patience has never been more unpredictable. Revenue growth, profit margins, and customer backlogs at Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure will be closely scrutinized. But the costs of the race will also be destiny determinants, as investors question the massive sums of capital being deployed and the timeline for seeing a return on the investment.

Last Thursday, Google parent Alphabet’s stock cratered 7% after the company raised its capital-expenditure projections for the year and reported negative free cash flow in its second quarter. For Amazon and Microsoft, the two cloud computing leaders, getting an edge could hinge on who can convince investors that they can soak up all that investment and spin it into gold faster.

Luke Rahbari, CEO of Equity Armor Investments who holds both stocks across several portfolios, said that even the act of raising and allocating capital has become a competitive bloodsport.

“Whoever controls the money controls the winners,” said Rahbari. “You’ve got to soak up as much money as you can so there isn’t as much money available to other players.”

Rahbari said he’ll be listening this week for signs of shakiness, and cracks in the voices of Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Amazon’s Andy Jassy, like the kind Rahbari made “when I had to call my parents from boarding school and tell them what kind of trouble I got into.”

“Frenemies”

Most investors are all in on both sides of the horse race. Amazon and Microsoft are two of the five largest weights in the S&P 500 with 8% to 9% of the index between them, so anyone investing for retirement has skin in the game. But the crux for any investor is that the massive spending must start flowing back to these companies as massive returns within the next few years. According to data from S&P Capital IQ, Microsoft’s stock trades at about 23 times expected earnings, cheaper than Amazon’s 27 times. Year-to-date, Microsoft’s stock is down 19%, while Amazon has been generally flat to up 2.5%.

Melissa Otto, global head of Visible Alpha research at S&P Global, described Amazon and Microsoft as competitors in a sense, but said she thinks of them more like “frenemies.” The hyperscaler market between Amazon Web Services, the name of Amazon’s cloud business, and Microsoft’s Azure cloud business operates largely with each holding a distinct slice. In her view, AWS is the flexible, customizable platform that is ideal for startups and for enormous machine learning workloads. It’s also more difficult to learn, she said. Azure extends the Microsoft software that enterprises already run, which makes it easier to adopt, she said.

In sum, the two have different strengths and chase different clients. When they do go after the same cohort of companies, customers often wind up buying both, she said.

The data, however, shows why it’s still essentially a horse race.

Between them, Microsoft and Amazon own half the cloud market, with Amazon’s 28% market share topping Microsoft’s 21%, according to Synergy data. Google Cloud, occupies the third spot, with its share of the market fluctuating between 12% and 14% depending on the quarter.

Based on Visible Alpha consensus estimates, AWS could reach $168 billion in net sales in 2026, up from last year’s $128.7 billion, a 30.7% rise. The margins AWS earns on that revenue, Otto said, “are sensational” at 93.8% gross margin, with a 35.4% operating margin expected. AWS has a current backlog of remaining performance obligations—signed customer contracts that will bring future revenue—of $364 billion, which excludes a recent $100 billion deal with Anthropic, Bank of America analysts wrote in a recent note, and said its in-house chip revenue commitments exceed $225 billion.

Microsoft’s Azure and its other cloud services are expected to reach $148.9 billion in the company’s fiscal 2027, up about 40% from roughly $106 billion in fiscal 2026, which ended in June. Still, Microsoft’s pace puts them slightly ahead of AWS, although it’s on a somewhat lower base, said Otto.

Microsoft doesn’t report metrics for Azure in the same way Amazon does for AWS. Visible Alpha estimates the Intelligent Cloud business earns an operating margin of about 47%, higher than AWS’s 35%. But that figure also includes older, higher-margin server software, so the actual number might be lower. Microsoft disclosed nearly $627 billion of remaining performance obligations which is 99% higher year-over-year, BofA analysts wrote. The RPO figure includes its entire commercial business, however, including Azure, M365, and Dynamics.

“Not only is [the Intelligent Cloud business] very profitable, it’s more profitable than AWS and growing faster,” Otto said, although that edge could be because enterprises are adopting AI and spending to keep up.

Still, it’s anyone’s game.

“We’re still extremely early days, so there isn’t really an established winner,” said Otto. “That’s why it’s such an arms race, because the incumbents don’t want to lose their edge.”

Both companies are plowing cash into their businesses, buying gear and building data centers to expand their cloud and AI services. Amazon’s free cash flow dropped to $1.2 billion during the past 12 months from $25.9 billion a year ago, and it more than doubled its bond debt to more than $120 billion. Microsoft isn’t issuing new bonds and is instead funding a buildout of roughly $35 billion per quarter from its operating cash flow. Its free cash flow for the 12 months ending in March was $73 billion, which was actually up slightly year-over-year, though analysts say comparing the cash flow directly to AWS is complicated because of the different ways the two companies’ finances are structured.

The Longshot

For Microsoft, the cloud race began as a longshot, as Nadella described recently.

“I remember when I became CEO, everybody said, oh my God, isn’t it too late man? Like, why even bother to build a public cloud because Amazon is so far ahead,” Nadella recalled at a Morgan Stanley conference in March. “We knew it was going to be multiplayer. We knew that there is going to be margin, and we kept building.”

The building has now reached a scale that investors could never have predicted. Amazon has guided to about $200 billion in capital expenditures across the company in 2026. Microsoft spent $104 billion in the first nine months of its fiscal year 2026, and is expected to land near $190 billion for the calendar year, based on guidance from CFO Amy Hood in April.

Jassy has told shareholders the AWS spending is almost all spoken for, including a commitment from OpenAI of more than $100 billion.

“We’re not investing approximately $200 billion in capex in 2026 on a hunch,” he wrote in his annual letter to investors. “Of the AWS capex we expect to spend in 2026, much of which will be monetized in 2027-2028, we already have customer commitments for a substantial portion of it.”

AWS has to splash out cash on land, power, and compute about six to 24 months before it can bill customers for cloud services, he wrote.

“The more capacity we open up, we sell it immediately,” Matt Wood, AWS’s chief AI and Technology officer told Fortune.

Nadella’s conviction on the massive investment rests on software, the backbone of Microsoft. Asked in March at the Morgan Stanley conference how to think about the return on all the capital Microsoft is spending, he offered a three-pronged answer that includes diverse customers, strong utilization, and a multi-generation total cost of ownership curve.

“We have OpenAI book, we have Anthropic book, but we want to also have the long tail of enterprise IT,” Nadella said.

With both Microsoft and Amazon neck-and-neck, the two cloud businesses are are selling out of everything they can build.

According to Amazon’s Wood, the applications that will fund returns are still newborns. The handful of available breakout AI products include chat assistants and coding tools, much like the early days of the internet when there were only a few websites.

“We’re going to have millions of them, just like we have millions of websites today,” said Wood. Efficiency gets customers in the door, but “there are going to be entirely new categories of products that just didn’t exist a year ago that are going to be absolute breakthrough smash hits.”

Both companies are selling everything they can build and throwing everything they have at building as fast as they possibly can. Whether that converts into the returns investors are waiting for gets its next test this week.

text:
SoftBank Group’s $40 billion bridge loan for its investment in U.S. tech giant OpenAI has attracted a new group of 21 lenders in a broader syndication phase, according to people familiar with the matter.

The group, which adds to the number of financial institutions already on the deal, has been allocated around $7 billion of the facility in total, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing a private matters. Out of that, First Abu Dhabi Bank, GIC and Standard Chartered Bank have each taken a nearly $1 billion share, said the people. The rest of the amount was allocated to European, Japanese and Taiwanese banks, the people added.

The number of new lenders was calculated on the parent level of each institution as some lenders are joining across more than one branch.

The remaining $33 billion of the bridge loan is held by underwriters and senior lenders, but it may be syndicated further, the people said. It is common for the initial lenders on a deal to distribute loans to a broader group.

The 12-month loan, signed in March, is one of the largest-ever bridge financings in the Asia-Pacific region, and is set to generate more than $100 million in fees for underwriters. The facility had already attracted nine new banks before it was launched into general syndication in May, despite concerns among some bankers over SoftBank’s exposure to OpenAI, which is facing increasing competition from rivals including Anthropic.

SoftBank, First Abu Dhabi Bank, Standard Chartered Bank and GIC declined to comment.

The bridge deal would pay an initial interest margin of about 250 basis points over the Secured Overnight Financing Rate. That would mean an interest rate of 6.14% at current SOFR levels.

SoftBank founder and CEO Masayoshi Son has pledged to go “all in” on OpenAI, with commitments now exceeding $60 billion. OpenAI filed for a public listing last month and was valued at $852 billion in a fundraising round in March.

text:
Fast-moving consumer trends are helping shape the brand's global strategy.

Levi Strauss & Co. is using the East Asia Pacific (EAP) region to refine retail and product strategies as it expands beyond jeans into a premium lifestyle brand.

“EAP is one of the most exciting places in the world to learn from and to build from,” Vicky Skelton, managing director for EAP at Levi Strauss & Co., told Retail Asia.

She said the region's high consumer expectations, sophisticated retail environment, and fast-changing culture make it “the perfect region to test and to learn as we establish the next chapter for Levi's.”

Skelton said each market serves a different purpose. Japan leads in premium craftsmanship, South Korea reflects rapid cultural shifts, Australia and New Zealand showcase denim across everyday and premium occasions, whilst Southeast Asia offers opportunities amongst younger consumers.

“It’s not one thing, it’s not one growth story, and that's what makes it so powerful,” she said in a video call.

Beyond its growth potential, Skelton said EAP allows Levi's to refine successful strategies before applying them more broadly because consumer trends evolve quickly and retail standards remain high across the region.

Levi's reported second-quarter Asia revenue of $284m, up 10% year on year, or 12% on an organic basis, whilst operating income rose 44% to $43m, according to its July filing. Direct-to-consumer revenue in Asia increased 12%.

Levi's is also broadening its business beyond denim bottoms into a premium lifestyle brand.

“The biggest shift right now is the way that we're building Levi's from a denim bottoms brand into a premium denim head-to-toe lifestyle brand, still rooted in our iconic products, but with a broader head-to-toe proposition,” Skelton said.

The company is expanding into categories such as outerwear, bags, accessories, and woven apparel as consumers increasingly look for complete outfit solutions.

Women's apparel is another priority alongside premiumisation.

“The opportunity for EAP is to make women’s [apparel] as strongly associated with Levi's as Levi's has been with men's over time,” she said.

Skelton said Japan has become the company's benchmark for premium products, with collections such as Blue Tab and Levi's Vintage Clothing performing well.

“Japan gives us that North Star for premium craft and heritage,” she said.

She added that premiumisation is about improving products, stores, digital experiences, and customer service rather than simply charging higher prices.

Despite weaker discretionary spending, Skelton said consumers continue to gravitate towards trusted brands that deliver lasting value.

Levi's expects growth to come from expanding its direct-to-consumer and omnichannel lines, boosting its women's offering, optimising its store network, and continuing its transition into a premium denim lifestyle brand.

“The brands that win in Asia are the globally consistent and locally meaningful brands, and that is exactly the balance that we want to instill across the region,” Skelton said.

text:
Joby Aviation and Virgin Atlantic signed a definitive agreement at the Farnborough International Airshow, formalizing a partnership first announced in 2025 to bring Joby’s electric air taxi service to the UK. The binding, multi-year commercial framework establishes Virgin Atlantic as Joby’s exclusive airline partner for air taxi services in the country.

The partnership builds on Joby’s existing relationship with Delta Air Lines, which holds a 49 percent stake in Virgin Atlantic, bringing together three brands focused on faster, more convenient travel across the UK. Under the agreement, Virgin Atlantic will offer Joby’s air taxi service through its booking platforms, including its mobile app and website, allowing UK travelers to book air taxi connections alongside their long-haul flights. Joby plans to launch service at Virgin Atlantic’s hubs in London and Manchester, with Manchester anchoring connections across the North of England. Early routes are expected to include Manchester Airport to Leeds in approximately 15 minutes and Heathrow to Central London in as little as 8 minutes, journeys that currently take over an hour by car.

Joby will retain sole responsibility for aircraft operations, route management, and securing regulatory approvals from the UK Civil Aviation Authority, while Virgin Atlantic will support infrastructure integration and customer acquisition at both hubs. Joby said it expects to expand the network to additional UK cities and communities over time. Earlier in July, the public had the opportunity to see a full-scale model of Joby’s aircraft at Potters Fields Park in London, across from Tower Bridge.

Joby’s aircraft uses six tilting propellers to take off and land vertically with a fraction of the noise produced by helicopters, and is optimized for rapid, back-to-back flights on routes of up to 100 miles. The company has completed thousands of test flights, including recent demonstrations in San Francisco and a point-to-point flight between JFK Airport and Manhattan in New York City. Joby’s aircraft certification is progressing under the Bilateral Aviation Safety Agreement between the FAA and UK CAA, building on the company’s 2022 validation application. Virgin Atlantic, founded in 1984, employs 9,250 people worldwide and flies to 28 destinations, operating a transatlantic network alongside Delta Air Lines that connects to more than 200 cities globally.

KEY QUOTES:

“This agreement marks an exciting next chapter in our partnership with Joby and a significant step towards bringing electric air taxi services to the UK. Together, we’ll create more seamless journeys for our customers, making it easier than ever to travel between towns, cities and our airports. Innovation has always been part of Virgin Atlantic’s DNA, and we’re proud to partner with Joby to help shape the future of travel while delivering the premium customer experience we’re known for.”

Corneel Koster, CEO, Virgin Atlantic

“Virgin Atlantic’s dedication to a world-class customer experience makes them the right partner to represent Joby in the UK, and this agreement reflects the next step in that relationship. The UK is one of the most exciting markets for this technology, and this partnership could drive significant opportunities for Joby as we bring air taxi service to some of the country’s busiest cities.”

title: IBM's $10 Billion Quantum Bet Can't Mask the Pain of a Historic Mainframe Rout ()
description:
On July 14, shares of Big Blue cratered more than 25% — eclipsing even the 23% plunge on Black Monday in 1987.
Krishna’s central thesis: this is a demand shift, not demand destruction.
A Quantum Leap — But Not a Quick Fix While the software and mainframe drama dominates headlines, IBM is trying to change the conversation.
On July 23, the company announced a binding agreement to acquire HRL Laboratories, a research facility previously owned by Boeing and General Motors.
The deal is part of a $10 billion, five-year investment plan focused on silicon spin qubits and quantum sensing.
text:
The numbers from IBM’s latest quarter were ugly enough to trigger the worst single-day selloff in the company’s 115-year history. But the real debate on Wall Street is whether the damage is temporary or structural.

On July 14, shares of Big Blue cratered more than 25% — eclipsing even the 23% plunge on Black Monday in 1987. The trigger was a rare pre-announcement from CEO Arvind Krishna, who warned that second-quarter momentum had stalled as customers diverted capital into scarce AI servers and memory chips. When the full results landed the following Wednesday, they confirmed the worst: revenue of $17.16 billion missed the $17.58 billion consensus, adjusted earnings per share of $2.93 came in below the $2.97 estimate, and net income fell to $2.17 billion.

The carnage was concentrated in hardware. Infrastructure revenue dropped 7% to $3.84 billion, with the flagship Z-mainframe business collapsing 42%. Software, by contrast, grew 5% to $7.76 billion, while consulting was flat at $5.33 billion. The company subsequently trimmed its full-year outlook to 4-5% constant-currency growth, down from its earlier forecast of “more than 5%.”

By Friday, the stock had stabilized, closing at €188.38 — a 3.74% gain for the session but still just 7.56% above the 52-week low of €175.14 hit on July 23. The 14-day RSI of 35.5 signals a stock hovering near oversold territory, and the annualized 30-day volatility of nearly 85% leaves little room for complacency.

Management Goes on the Defensive

In the aftermath, IBM’s top brass has been working the phones. CFO Jim Kavanaugh pushed back against fears that customers are abandoning mainframes, telling Yahoo Finance that key indicators point to a potential record year relative to prior upgrade cycles. CEO Arvind Krishna echoed that message in a CNBC interview on July 23, arguing that AI coding tools and competitors won’t displace IBM’s software business.

Krishna’s central thesis: this is a demand shift, not demand destruction. Only 2% of IBM’s software portfolio is truly vulnerable to AI-driven displacement, he contends, while the remaining 98% remains essential — customers need those tools to build their own AI infrastructure. If he’s right, the market is pricing a temporary dent. If he’s wrong, IBM faces a structural problem no quarterly report can paper over.

The stock’s year-to-date decline of 27.52% suggests investors remain skeptical.

A Quantum Leap — But Not a Quick Fix

While the software and mainframe drama dominates headlines, IBM is trying to change the conversation. On July 23, the company announced a binding agreement to acquire HRL Laboratories, a research facility previously owned by Boeing and General Motors. The deal is part of a $10 billion, five-year investment plan focused on silicon spin qubits and quantum sensing.

By 2029, IBM aims to reshape the enterprise landscape with this technology. Ambitious — but the timeline extends far beyond the current earnings crisis. Quantum computing won’t solve a single one of the problems that sent the stock into a tailspin in July.

Analysts Split on the Path Forward

Wall Street is divided. Susquehanna’s James Friedman slashed his price target from $303 to $225 but kept a “Neutral” rating. Morgan Stanley raised its target by roughly 10% after the initial warning, before the full numbers were out. Stifel’s David Grossman sees the stock grinding sideways with a slight downward bias, citing low visibility into coming quarters and seasonal headwinds.

The consensus analyst target of €231.06 implies meaningful upside — if the “software pause” proves temporary. But with the stock trading 35.67% below its 52-week high of €292.85, the recovery path is anything but straight.

What Comes Next

The digestion of the earnings shock is largely complete. The focus now shifts to two questions: whether deferred large-scale deals close in the coming months, and whether Red Hat and the watsonx software suite can offset ongoing weakness in infrastructure. The bull case hinges on the idea that the current AI infrastructure boom in servers and chips doesn’t extend deep into 2027, allowing companies to redirect spending back to mainframe capacity.

For now, Krishna’s “shift, not destruction” narrative is the only game in town. The next few quarters will determine whether it’s a lifeline or a last resort.

title: United CEO Scott Kirby Pitched Delta On A Merger — One Airline Would Control 35% Of ...
description:
United Airlines pitched a merger to Delta Air Lines according to new reporting in the Wall Street Journal.
This comes alongside United having pitched the idea of taking over American Airlines in an Oval Office meeting with the President.
In the case of Delta, There’s no case that the Atlanta-based carrier is an undervalued asset.
Foreign Governments Won’t Stand For It The Delta-Air France-KLM-Virgin Atlantic joint venture together has a 25% seat share in the North Atlantic.
This casts Scott Kirby’s efforts to take over American Airlines in new light.
text:
United Airlines pitched a merger to Delta Air Lines according to new reporting in the Wall Street Journal. United CEO Scott Kirby called his counterpart at Delta Ed Bastian. Delta did “preliminary due diligence” on a tie-up, but the conversations didn’t bear fruit.

This comes alongside United having pitched the idea of taking over American Airlines in an Oval Office meeting with the President. American’s board rejected the offer, and by explaining that it was dead on arrival because the deal would be too anticompetitive basically killed prospects by providing admissions for any potential antitrust case against it.

There’s No Business Case For This Deal

Combining Delta and United would make the largest U.S. and world airline by a wide margin. But it wouldn’t solve a problem that either has, or make better use of either’s assets than each one makes of them on their own. In fact, any deal would be subractive – they would have to give up some of their best assets to appease regulators and the courts (if this were even possible).

At least with American there was a plausible argument that the Dallas-based carrier has financially underperformed and United management might make those assets perform better. In the case of Delta,

There’s no case that the Atlanta-based carrier is an undervalued asset. It is generally more profitable and valued by investors than United.

There’s no case that the Atlanta-based carrier is poorly-run, so combining it with United gives better management (and therefore profitable results) to those assets.

There’s no case that United or Delta on their own are too undersized to be viable, so a combination is necessary for them to succeed.

Instead, and bolstered by Kirby’s apparently agnosticism towards merging with either Delta or American, it’s pure hubris – a desire to get bigger rather than earn outsized return on capital for shareholders.

The Antitrust Hurdles Would Be Unimaginable

The idea of a Delta-United merger is a complete antitrust non-starter, and that’s even assuming getting an antitrust pass from the Trump administration (both United and Delta donated $1 million to President Trump’s inauguration, and Kirby even publicly supported the President’s tariffs which were harmful to United’s international-heavy business, and publicly blasted Democrats for obstruction in the fall government shutdown.

Each state attorney general has their own independent cause of action (except, arguably, Delaware – Wilmington is served only by Avelo – and perhaps New Hampshire which has United but not Delta service).

Myriad counteries get a bite at the antitrust apple as well.

Delta has 18% of the domestic U.S. market, United has 17%. Together they’re nearly 35%. By scheduled seats they’d reach 37% (because United and Delta operate longer flights on average than Southwest).

United and Delta each control about 24% of the New York market, and together would have 48.6%. Twenty New York – Europe city pairs have both United and Delta service. United is 16% of LAX and Delta is 19%, together representing 35%.

Delta and United together own more than one-third of Republic Airways Holdings, the primary competitor to SkyWest in the regional market, and both contract with SkyWest – which would itself lose significant bargaining leverage.

United has a 40% stake in CommuteAir and Delta owns Endeavor Air outright. Perhaps now we know why United was so adamant about getting its flight attendants to agree to its ownership of a commuter carrier (without staffing them with United’s union flight attendants) in their recently-approved contract.

Foreign Governments Won’t Stand For It

The Delta-Air France-KLM-Virgin Atlantic joint venture together has a 25% seat share in the North Atlantic. The United-Air Canada-Lufthansa Group joint venture has a 28% share. United and Delta on their own would be 24%. Add United to Delta’s joint venture and that’s 37%. Add Delta to United’s joint venture and that’s 40%. There’s no world in which European regulators ascent to this.

In South America the two overlap on New York – São Paulo. Via different hubs, the two networks compete to São Paulo, Buenos Aires, Rio, Bogotá, Lima and Santiago. Delta’s joint venture with LATAM substantially broadens this, creating antitrust problems across South America (before Delta partnered with LATAM, American faced huge antitrust resistance to a joint venture with them – adding United into the mix likely kills the joint venture, and might not review even without it).

Japanese and Australian regulators are likely to have issues with the tie-up, and it could jeopardize Delta’s joint venture with Korean Air and United’s with ANA and Air New Zealand.

United and Air Canada dominate the transborder Canada market. Delta and Aeromexico – already facing legal challenge from DOT – are the dominant force between the U.S. and Mexico.

The two airlines would have to give up crown jewel partnerships but even then might not satisfy regulators in any given market. It’s unclear the U.K. would approve the combination even if Delta divested Virgin Atlantic. They might not be able to retain their full portfolio of Haneda slots, if United tried to retain its ANA relationship. There’s already virtually no competition with Korean and Delta between North America and Seoul. The little competition that exists is mostly from United.

Ownership Stakes In Foreign Airlines Further Complicate Matters

Things get even more complicated when you look at ownership stakes. Delta has a 49% stake in Virgin Atlantic, 19% stake in Aeromexico, 15% of Korean Air, 13% of WestJet, 11% of LATAM, 3% of Air France and 2% of China Eastern.

United owns 9% of Azul, and stakes in Avianca and Gol via Abra Group and they’re a minority investor in JSX.

A Merger Would Erode Delta’s Key Competitive Advantage

A United merger would almost certainly mean unionization across Delta. Today, only pilots and flight dispatchers are unionized. Flight attendants, airport agents and reservationists who provide customer service are non-union. Mechanics, whom Delta has turned into an independent profit center are non-union. These represent competitive advantages for the business which any merger with a similar-sized carrier would almost certainly erode.

The Two Airlines Haven’t Partnered Since 2003

Delta and United did actually used to be partners. I used to credit my Delta Air Lines flights to Mileage Plus! The two had a frequent flyer partnership that ran 1998 – 2003, and they intended codesharing which was killed by Delta pilots. The deal ended as United aligned with US Airways and Delta with Northwest and Continental.

They were both much smaller then. Delta and Northwest hadn’t merged. United and Continental hadn’t merged. There were several more players in the domestic market.

This casts Scott Kirby’s efforts to take over American Airlines in new light. It isn’t about taking American, an underperforming asset, and making the two great together. It’s about buying whatever larger airline he can – less as an investment and more just to be the biggest by a wide margin. And since his Delta entreaties apparently came last year, American may even have been his second choice.

text:
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby reportedly approached Delta Air Lines last year to discuss a potential merger that would have created the world's largest airline by market value. According to an exclusive Wall Street Journal report, Kirby personally contacted Delta CEO Ed Bastian as United explored another blockbuster consolidation opportunity after years of pursuing ambitious growth strategies. The discussions ultimately went no further, with both airlines moving on from the proposal in different directions.

The revelation comes months after reports emerged that Kirby had also floated the idea of merging United with American Airlines, as previously covered by Simple Flying. While neither proposal advanced, the latest report highlights the United chief executive's willingness and ambition to pursue industry-defining transactions despite the enormous regulatory hurdles such deals would face.

United's Latest Megadeal Ambition

According to people familiar with the matter cited by The Wall Street Journal, Kirby contacted Bastian directly as part of United's proposal to combine the two largest and most profitable US network airlines. Delta's leadership reportedly evaluated the approach and conducted preliminary due diligence before deciding not to move forward with formal discussions. Both sides eventually abandoned the idea.

The proposed combination would have united two airlines that have become dominant forces in the US market following decades of industry consolidation. However, aviation executives have long viewed a United-Delta merger as virtually impossible because of likely opposition from antitrust regulators, given the carriers' combined market power that would have created a monopoly across domestic and international routes.

The Wall Street Journal wrote the following regarding the deal:

"The talks didn't progress, and both companies later moved on from the proposal."

Why Delta Was An Attractive Target

The report suggests Kirby's interest reflected more than simple market expansion. Delta has long been regarded as the industry's benchmark for profitability, premium customer experience, and operational reliability, with overall good passenger reviews. Kirby has repeatedly praised Delta's strategy, which emphasizes attracting higher-yield travelers rather than competing primarily on low fares.

That philosophy has significantly influenced United's own transformation over recent years. The carrier has invested heavily in premium cabins, lounges, international connectivity, and onboard products as it attempts to narrow the performance gap with Delta. According to the report, United and Delta together generated more than 90% of the US airline industry's profits last year, illustrating how dominant the two airlines have become.

Financially, the combined company would also have been enormous. The Wall Street Journal reported that Delta's market value stood at roughly $56 billion, while United was valued at around $38 billion at the time of publication, creating a business with unprecedented scale of almost $100 billion in the US airline sector. But the deal remains theoretical.

Regulatory Obstacles Remain Overwhelming For Mega Mergers

Even if Delta had shown greater interest, completing such a merger would likely have proven extraordinarily difficult, or probably impossible. The four largest US airlines, such as the Big Three: American, Delta, United, plus Southwest and JetBlue, already dominate the domestic aviation market after a wave of consolidation during the past two decades. A merger between United and Delta would almost certainly have triggered intense scrutiny from the Department of Justice, state attorneys general, and other competition authorities.

The timing of the proposal is also notable. According to the report, some business leaders believed the second Trump administration might take a more accommodating approach toward large corporate mergers than previous administrations. Even so, the sheer size of a United-Delta combination would have made regulatory approval highly uncertain.

The proposal also followed reports that Kirby had explored another industry-changing transaction involving American Airlines. That earlier idea attracted criticism from lawmakers, while President Donald Trump reportedly expressed opposition and American Airlines CEO Robert Isom publicly described such a combination as "anticompetitive." It means that the Big Three continue to be separate and rivals in the skies over the US and abroad with no imminent merger possibility.

text:
Waymo, the autonomous driving company under Alphabet, has notified Uber of a breakup after three years. Announcing that it will enter the market independently, Waymo has effectively begun the process of ending the partnership.

According to the Financial Times on the 26th, Waymo has been internally discussing plans to end its current contract with Uber. The two companies currently operate services in Austin and Atlanta in the United States. In a statement, Uber said, "Waymo has notified us that it will enter the two markets independently in January 2028, when the contract permits." The deterioration in the two companies' relationship is the result of a lobbying war over the future of robotaxis.

The two companies, which first joined hands in 2023, fell out as they emerged as direct competitors in some markets. Both have been lobbying for robotaxi legislation favorable to themselves while keeping each other in check. "The two companies are pursuing different goals," one official said.

The dissolution of the partnership deals a major blow to Uber's autonomous driving plans. After selling its own autonomous driving division in 2020, Uber has invested more than $10 billion (about 14.6 trillion won) over the past year in equity stakes and robotaxi vehicle contracts to close the gap it had fallen behind on.

Uber's shares have fallen more than 16% this year. Investor concerns that it could be overtaken by autonomous vehicle (AV) companies played a part. On news of Waymo's exit, the share price fell more than 4% on the 24th.

Waymo is already eroding Uber's market share in some cities, including San Francisco. It currently operates more than 3,800 vehicles in 10 cities. In February, it raised $16 billion (about 23.4 trillion won) at a valuation of $126 billion (about 184 trillion won).

"From Cleanliness to School Buses": Uber-Waymo "Betrayal of the Alliance" Turns to All-Out War

The two companies also differed over service quality. Waymo raised issues with the cleanliness and routing of Uber-operated vehicles. Uber, on the other hand, countered that it had been constrained in deployment. In May, dozens of Waymo vehicles blocked a dead-end street in Atlanta, sparking controversy—and Uber was responsible for the vehicle routing.

Uber pointed out that the financial terms of the contract were unsustainable and that Waymo vehicles suddenly became unavailable during severe weather. In December, after a series of incidents in Austin in which vehicles drove past stopped school buses, Uber sent a letter to Waymo.

The conflict peaked as Uber called on regulators for a so-called "hybrid network" in which drivers and autonomous vehicles operate on the same platform. In New Jersey, Uber lobbyists proposed that a robotaxi service platform should have human drivers handle more than 85% of all operations during a three-year pilot period.

Experts analyzed that this rule would force AV companies with their own apps—such as Tesla, Waymo, and Amazon-owned Zoox—to provide services through third-party apps. Grayson Brulte, co-founder of the data firm Autonomy AI, pointed out, "Uber is trying to buy time through regulatory capture," adding, "It's just a move to protect its market share."

Uber countered, "It is not true that we are anti-AV or trying to slow the spread of AV." It said that a hybrid network "delivers the technology to consumers faster while providing policymakers with a practical framework for managing the transition."

text:
Chinese fast-fashion e-commerce giant SHEIN published its initial public offering (IPO) prospectus via the Hong Kong Stock Exchange website on July 26. According to sources familiar with the matter, if all goes smoothly, the listing is expected between late August and early September, with proceeds planned for IT investments including artificial intelligence (AI).

The prospectus revealed detailed financials for the first time, showing revenue for the fiscal year ended December 2025 expanded 8% year-over-year to $41.8 billion (approximately ¥6.8 trillion), while net profit fell 38.7% from the prior year to $2.064 billion (approximately ¥340 billion). While the company has sustained rapid growth, a clear deceleration is evident on the profitability front.

Financial Highlights

SHEIN's performance over the past three fiscal years, as detailed in the prospectus, is as follows:

Fiscal YearRevenue ($B)Net Profit ($B)Net Profit MarginFY202332.1Not disclosedNot disclosedFY202438.73.3658.7%FY202541.82.0644.9%

Net profit margins are calculated from figures disclosed in the prospectus. While revenue increased for a second consecutive year, net profit for FY2025 declined approximately 39% from the prior year, with the net profit margin dropping 3.8 percentage points from 8.7% to 4.9%. The company has grown through a low-cost, on-demand model that starts with small-batch production of as few as 100 units of apparel manufactured in China, then places additional orders based on sales performance. However, intensifying competition and rising logistics costs may be squeezing profitability.

The deterioration in profitability also reflects the erosion of a key premise underlying its business model. SHEIN had shipped goods directly from warehouses in China to consumers in the U.S. and Europe, leveraging the low per-unit value of shipments to circumvent tariffs. However, the company was dealt a blow when the U.S. abolished the "de minimis" rule, which had exempted low-value shipments under $800 from duties. According to the Financial Times, the EU and the UK are also moving to eliminate similar exemptions. Low pricing—SHEIN's greatest weapon—is being undermined on the regulatory front.

A Winding Road to Listing and Use of Proceeds

SHEIN's IPO plans have undergone numerous twists and turns over an extended period. The company initially aimed for a listing on the New York Stock Exchange but abandoned that path due to deteriorating U.S.-China relations and regulatory hurdles. It subsequently explored a listing on the London Stock Exchange, but that also failed to materialize.

Valuation Trajectory and Fundraising Scale

Over the four years leading up to the listing, the company's valuation has been significantly marked down. According to reports from the FT and other media, SHEIN was valued at $100 billion during a share sale in 2022, but that figure was lowered to approximately $66 billion in a funding round in May 2023. Subsequently, some investors called for a further reduction to around $30 billion. The Hong Kong listing is expected to carry a valuation in the range of $40 billion to $50 billion—less than half its peak level.

The CSRC announcement indicated that the maximum number of shares to be issued in Hong Kong is 341.6 million, with expected proceeds of up to $3 billion.

Market Environment and Significance of the Listing

SHEIN's IPO is expected to be one of the largest deals in the retail sector in several years. With many consumer brands postponing IPOs amid weak investor sentiment and a slowdown in spending by middle- and lower-income consumers, SHEIN's move is drawing significant market attention.

The company has established a business model dubbed "ultra-fast fashion," leveraging China's flexible supply chain with the U.S. and Europe as its primary markets. It has grown into a competitor challenging established fast-fashion brands such as Inditex (ITX.MC), which operates Zara, and H&M (HM-B.ST).

That said, a significant gap remains when comparing profitability with established incumbents. Compared against the most recent full-year results of its peers, SHEIN's net profit margin falls even below that of H&M.

Due to differing fiscal year-ends, this is not a strictly like-for-like comparison; Inditex and H&M figures are based on their respective full-year earnings releases. Nevertheless, as the sharp decline in net profit illustrates, profitability challenges are emerging behind the rapid expansion. The valuation that the Hong Kong market assigns will be the key focus going forward.

SHEIN currently operates as a private company. Through this IPO, it aims to raise external capital and accelerate AI investments, positioning itself to transition to the next phase of growth.

text:
The launch of the latest AI model from a Chinese company — Moonshot AI’s Kimi — reignited debates around American competitiveness and open versus proprietary AI.

While there was plenty of conversation on social media, it seems the debate is also happening behind the scenes in Washington, D.C., where OpenAI and Anthropic have reportedly lobbied regulators with concern about open Chinese models.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed why this seems to be such a hot button issue. Beyond suggesting that certain folks should “touch grass” rather than spending their weekends arguing on X, Sean noted that in many ways, this “feels like we’re seeing repeats of prior freakouts,” with everyone in Silicon Valley “expecting that something is going to arrive and blow everything else away.”

And Kirsten noted that putting heavy restrictions on Chinese AI models could primarily benefit a handful of companies: “Are we accelerating and ensuring that Americans win the AI race, or are we ensuring that certain frontier labs do better than others?

Keep reading for an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Anthony Ha: For folks who have followed the discourse around Chinese AI, this will probably be very, very familiar from the launch of DeepSeek, where basically a Chinese model comes out; on some benchmarks, it does as well, or at least seems competitive with some of the frontier models; and a certain portion of the tech industry loses their mind.

Some of this [debate] got extra scrutiny because one of the people posting about it was [an executive] at OpenAI. But in general, there [is] this recurring question of: Can Chinese companies beat US companies, at least in some aspects, and do it much more cheaply and in a much more open way?

Sean O’Kane: Yeah, there are many elements of this that feel like we’re seeing repeats of prior freakouts. I think one of my favorites is: Everybody is so ready [for] and so expecting that something is going to arrive and blow everything else away. And I think my favorite example of that this past week was people showing off that “My gosh, Kimi made in 30 minutes an entire replication of macOS.” And yeah, it made a pretty impressive graphical reproduction of what macOS looks like, but it’s not an OS.

We keep seeing these things happen over and over again, where everybody’s so jumpy in the tech industry. And I think in particular, with some of the Chinese models that come out, there’s this expectation, and I think this gets to the core of why people reacted the way they reacted last weekend. (Also, by the way: Go outside, touch grass, it’s the weekend. Everybody in the industry was trading barbs on Twitter all weekend.) But this jumpiness is really interesting to me because we’re now a week out and I don’t think anybody’s feeling like the end is nigh like they were a week ago.

Kirsten Korosec: We have a really great story by one of our reporters, Tim Fernholz, who tries to unpack the psychosis around this here in the United States. He points to a number of reasons. And concludes — and I don’t want to conclude it for him, but I think that there’s one that rises more to the top than others.

There’s concerns that these Chinese open weight models might have an implicit bias towards China, there’s another worry about security risks and guardrails. But there’s also a pretty big idea here, which is protectionism, and who is going to quote-unquote “win the race”? Is it going to be the US or China? And that seems to be driving a lot of what the fear is.

I don’t know, Anthony, if you agree with that?

Anthony: I completely agree. I think the China aspect always adds this certain level of hysteria. And that’s not to say that people shouldn’t be concerned about how the U.S. stacks up against China across different industries. But it gets so amped up.

The other thing this reminds me of is the discussion around TikTok a few years ago. And again, it wasn’t that I thought that the concerns around TikTok were totally made up, but that the level of how panicked people got — it seems as soon as you add the word China to any discussion, things just ramp up dramatically. And then in this case, it’s linked to this discussion about open [weights] and this idea that AI is so powerful and so dangerous that the only way we can control it is with these proprietary models from these American frontier companies.

Obviously, most people saying this [have] reasons why they want to say that. David Sacks, who was the AI czar for the Trump administration [and] now has a different role in the Trump administration, was shouting on X about how, “I can’t believe people are opposing data centers, we’re tying ourselves in knots, there’s too much regulation.” And so it’s a way to argue for the positions that they already had around AI. “My gosh, if China beats us, that’s unthinkable, so you have to do what I want to do anyway.”

Kirsten: Right, and if you were to put across-the-board bans on Chinese open weight models — I’m not saying that there aren’t real concerns here, but let’s just play that out. If we were to do that, it would benefit models created by OpenAI, for instance, and it would force enterprises to use those as opposed to using models like Kimi.

So you really have to ask the question: Are we accelerating and ensuring that Americans win the AI race, or are we ensuring that certain frontier labs do better than others?

Sean: At this point, we should say a lot of this discussion really got kicked off by the head of strategic futures at OpenAI, Dean Ball, who was the first one to come out with this really long post mentioning some of these concerns.

Part of me thinks the reaction to this was because people disagreed with what Dean wrote. Part of me also thinks the reaction was driven by the fact that he kind of just said the thing out loud. He basically said the US should create regulatory FUD — fear, uncertainty, and doubt — and muck up the ability for these open weight models to compete with the US. [Ball later backed away from this argument.]

And to me, I think you can read in some of the responses from folks, like, “You’re not supposed to say that out loud, Dean.”

text:
United Airlines wanted to merge with fellow U.S airline and fierce rival Delta, but talks collapsed, and a combination never progressed.

The exclusive report flagged by The Wall Street Journal tested one of the, but not the only, audacious ideas in recent U.S. aviation history: two of the largest airlines possibly coming together.

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, just like his push for American Airlines at the front of the dialogue, called Delta CEO Ed Bastian in 2025 and expressed his desire for a combination.

What Happened Between United and Delta?

Per WSJ, Kirby’s interest in Delta came in 2025 and centred on a discussion of a possible deal to merge the airlines within the United States. The approach was more exploratory; it didn’t include a formal proposal or an approved plan from the board, but that didn’t erode the seriousness of the effort.

The conversations, however, did not progress far, similar to the ones Kirby held at American Airlines at the beginning of 2026. Delta’s leadership team reportedly rejected the idea; no formal negotiations were opened, and the story broke in July 2026.

Despite months having passed, Delta’s interest remains at zero, with no intent to bring the two large companies together in a dominating transaction that would reshape the U.S. market.

Delta viewed itself as a successful independent airline that would not need consolidation to survive. United’s move, therefore, while ambitious, ended very quickly, and not because regulators had weighed in, but rather because its move was not of interest.

Naturally, after Delta turned down United’s approach, some analysts expected consolidation to cool; however, that didn’t happen, with then-Kirby sounding out a merger with American Airlines to unite his and this U.S. carrier, just as had happened with Delta but failed.

Why United Airlines Wanted A Merger

For United Airlines, the logic behind its outreach comes amid not just its own ambition for the future but also the sense of opportunity in its competitors within the United States.

United Airlines has been trying to match Delta’s margins and return on invested capital for some time; while ambitious, it is always looking to track competitors, see where they’re doing well, and try to do better. A United and Delta combination was a way to leapfrog constraints and grow for the future.

If executed, the chance to eliminate overlapping capacity would’ve been possible; on paper, the cost synergies at airports from maintenance and even corporate sense could’ve been captured more efficiently.

The pair would’ve had the chance to complement hubs and international networks, leveraging each other’s existing successes in specific markets and continuing that trajectory. United has a strength in Asia and Delta in Latin America; mixing those strengths has rewarding possibilities.

Consolidation isn’t new within the U.S.; since deregulation, the sector has gone through wave after wave of consolidation efforts, with Northwest turning into Delta, Continental moving into United, and U.S. Airways becoming American, leaving the big three as they have been for multiple decades.

These big three have been able to stand on their own feet, even if pressure has impacted American Airlines’ performance across 2020 and further consolidation would, while being the next step based on previous moves, be considered by analysts dramatic, and by regulators something audacious.

Kirby has preached the strategic value of consolidation for some time; by May 2026, though, he shifted to downplaying the need for a mega-merger, even if his actions over the last 12 months don’t align with this.

While United doesn’t need a merger, testing the waters is a chance to see whether a mega-deal could reshape the competitive landscape and the global industry for generations.

Why The Merger Never Really Stood A Chance

When Scott Kirby phoned his friend and competitor, Ed Bastian of Delta, in 2025, the probability of his proposal being rejected was high, but that didn’t stop the approach and call from taking place.

Even if Delta had been interested in coming together, the barriers were always too high for the idea pitched by United Airlines. While Delta leadership needed to approve the concept first and foremost, that would’ve represented only the first pillar in what would have become a consolidation seen only once in a lifetime.

Regulatory opposition would’ve been one of the greatest barriers to any possible coming together. While there has been more openness under the current administration to companies coming together, that doesn’t mean aggressive merger intent will always get a clear pass.

A full corporate merger that extends beyond previous DOJ pushback from alliances like the Northeast between American and JetBlue shows the obstacles in the way. Two of the three largest U.S airlines coming together would’ve faced a wall of antitrust objections in every sector that makes up the fabric of being an airline.

Regulators would’ve wanted to understand the premise, long-term view, how the impact on customers would’ve been handled, competition, pricing, slots, airport gates, labour and more. All of these obstacles that companies at this scale face are challenging to overcome without significant resources and finances.

Barclays says a sharp slowdown in share buybacks by major U.S. technology companies is unlikely to weigh significantly on the broader equity market.

The brokerage argues that investors have increasingly rewarded growth over capital returns as artificial intelligence spending accelerates across the sector.

Big Tech companies are shifting capital allocation priorities to fund a multiyear AI infrastructure buildout, with hyperscaler capital expenditures expected to exceed $1 trillion annually by 2028.

Buybacks by the largest technology firms have already fallen about 17% over the past year, even as repurchases across the rest of the technology sector and the broader S&P 500 have continued to rise.

The six largest technology companies, including Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG), Amazon, and Meta, accounted for more than a quarter of all S&P 500 buybacks in 2024 and 2025.

The decline reflects growing funding needs for AI investments, with companies increasingly relying on debt issuance, equity offerings, convertible securities, and operating cash flow to finance expansion.

Barclays also noted that reduced stock-based compensation following aggressive workforce reductions may have lessened the need for buybacks among major technology firms.

Valuations for Big Tech have compressed from around 33 times earnings two years ago to below 25 times as investors factor in a prolonged and capital-intensive investment cycle.

Despite the pullback in buybacks, Barclays argued that the market’s focus has shifted decisively toward growth and long-term AI-driven returns over near-term shareholder distributions.

The data suggests investors are placing considerably greater value on companies reinvesting capital into AI-driven expansion rather than returning cash to shareholders through repurchase programs.

With hyperscaler spending projected to surpass $1 trillion annually within two years, the structural shift away from buybacks among the largest technology names appears set to continue well into the decade.

text:
Carrier Global Corp. (ISIN US1442851009) stock sits in a measured position between earnings-driven fundamentals and its long term climate-solutions strategy, offering investors a mix of cyclical exposure and structural HVAC demand according to the latest available financial data as of 2025.

Revenue trends frame Carrier Global stock

Carrier Global Corp., the climate and HVAC specialist spun out of United Technologies, reported multi billion dollar revenue in its latest full fiscal year, with the companys filings and investor presentations indicating that annual sales remained in the tens of billions of USD range as of fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025, driven by a diversified portfolio of residential HVAC, commercial systems, and refrigeration solutions across North America, Europe, and Asia.

According to public financial portals summarizing Carrier Global Corp.s results for fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025, the group recorded year on year revenue growth in the low to mid single digit percentage range, translating into hundreds of millions of dollars of additional annual sales versus the prior year period, as demand for energy efficient heating and cooling systems and regulatory pressure to reduce emissions supported orders from commercial building owners, data center operators, and cold chain logistics companies.

Investor materials for Carrier Global Corp. emphasize that the HVAC segment contributes the majority of revenue, with residential and light commercial units accounting for a significant share of sales in the United States and other developed markets in fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025, while the refrigeration segment provides exposure to food retail, transportation, and industrial applications in Europe and other regions.

Carrier Global Corp. has also highlighted the impact of inflation, supply chain normalization, and input cost dynamics on its revenue mix, noting that price increases on HVAC units and systems helped offset higher component and labor costs in the 2024 reporting period, thereby supporting nominal revenue growth even in markets with modest volume expansion.

Operating margin and earnings comparison support valuation

In addition to revenue trends, Carrier Global Corp.s operating margin and net earnings play a central role in how Carrier Global stock is valued by investors focused on industrial and building technology companies. Publicly available summaries of the companys fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025 results show that Carrier Global Corp. generated operating income and net income in the billions of USD, with operating margins in the low to mid teens as a percentage of sales, reflecting both favorable product mix and ongoing cost discipline.

Compared with the prior year, Carrier Global Corp.s latest reported fiscal results show changes in profitability metrics that investors watch closely. For example, in one recent fiscal year the company reported that its adjusted earnings per share increased by a mid single digit percentage versus the prior year, reflecting higher gross margin on premium HVAC products, efficiency gains in manufacturing, and a more favorable mix in commercial and refrigeration segments, while reported EPS was affected by restructuring charges and portfolio optimization costs.

Public data from financial portals also indicate that Carrier Global Corp.s net income margin, measured as net income divided by revenue, remained in a high single digit percentage band in the latest reporting year, broadly consistent with industrial peers focused on building technologies and climate solutions, and the comparison versus prior year margins shows a slight improvement, suggesting that the companys pricing actions and productivity programs are flowing through to the bottom line.

For investors analyzing Carrier Global stock, the quantified comparison between current and prior year earnings metrics underpins many valuation discussions. When net income rises by hundreds of millions of USD versus the preceding year and adjusted EPS moves higher by several percent, the stocks price to earnings multiple can be assessed against both internal history and external peer benchmarks, even though short term market sentiment and macroeconomic conditions can cause the share price to diverge from purely fundamental fair value estimates.

Carrier Global Corp. has also communicated leverage, cash flow, and capital allocation figures in its investor presentations, indicating that free cash flow for fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025 was sufficient to support debt reduction, selective acquisitions focused on digital building solutions, and shareholder returns via dividends and buybacks, providing another layer of fundamental support for Carrier Global stock beyond headline revenue and profit numbers.

HVAC and climate solutions drive long term growth

The long term appeal of Carrier Global stock is closely linked to structural demand for heating, ventilation, and air conditioning as well as broader climate solutions. Carrier Global Corp.s product portfolio includes a wide range of HVAC systems calibrated for energy efficiency, indoor air quality, and regulatory compliance, ranging from residential split systems and furnaces to large scale commercial chillers and rooftop units used in office buildings, schools, hospitals, and industrial facilities.

In public communications, the company has emphasized that global HVAC demand is supported by urbanization, rising living standards, and the trend toward electrification of heating and cooling, while the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and improve building energy performance creates additional impetus for customers to upgrade older equipment to high efficiency models. This narrative is backed by figures showing that a considerable portion of Carrier Global Corp.s revenue in recent years comes from replacement and retrofit markets, where customers move to newer systems with better seasonal energy efficiency ratios and lower lifecycle operating costs.

Carrier Global Corp.s refrigeration and cold chain solutions also form an important pillar of the business. The group supplies systems and components that keep food, pharmaceuticals, and other temperature sensitive goods within specified ranges in supermarkets, transport vehicles, and warehouses. Public data indicates that refrigeration units and related services contribute a significant percentage of overall revenue, providing diversification beyond HVAC and offering exposure to defensive end markets such as food retail and healthcare.
